mstts:express-as.prosody: As we wrap up our look at "Savage Inequalities," I want you to really sit with this: reading these stories, seeing the realities of America’s schools up close, it’s almost impossible not to feel both anger and hope all at once. The inequalities? They’re out in the open—etched into the very walls and daily routines of our schools. Still, maybe the most powerful thing this book gives us is the reminder that none of this is set in stone. These injustices—they’re the result of decisions, of priorities, of choices that we can change. If there’s one thing I hope you carry forward, it’s this: the fate of kids in our schools isn’t sealed. Every single day, in every community, there are people showing up, doing the hard work to make things better. Yes, it’s tough. Progress can be slow. But it matters. The future isn’t fixed—it’s shaped by what we choose to see, what we decide to value, and what we’re willing to fight for. So, let’s pull together the biggest lessons here: School funding that’s tied to property taxes? It just keeps inequality and segregation alive. When schools are underfunded day after day, hope shrinks, and kids’ futures get limited. Even the best reform ideas can fall flat if there’s no long-term commitment and real community support. But here’s the good news—grassroots efforts, the everyday heroes in our schools and neighborhoods, they really do make a difference. And this struggle for educational justice? It’s still going—it takes empathy, and it takes all of us, working together. The way forward isn’t about waiting for a miracle fix, or hoping for one person to save the day. It’s about showing up—again and again—for the kids who need us most. It’s about listening to voices that too often get ignored, and refusing to accept a world where a child’s zip code decides their future. Change starts when we’re honest about what’s really happening. When we ask tough questions. When we believe, deep down, that every child is worth the fight. And if you carry that belief—whether you’re a parent, a neighbor, a voter, or just someone who cares—you’re already part of the story of hope and change. The work ahead isn’t easy. But it’s necessary. And in the end, it’s the work of building a world that’s more just, more loving, and full of possibility for every child.
